statements: The chief complaint is a 6-month history of headache in a 49-year-old man.
The patient’s main concern appears to be chronic headache.
The key diagnostic issue is identifying the nature of the sellar/suprasellar cystic lesion found on imaging.
MRI shows an 18 × 14 × 14 mm sellar cystic lesion extending from the suprasellar cistern through the diaphragma sellae to the dorsum sellae.
The lesion compresses the optic chiasm.
The lesion is hypointense on T1-weighted MRI.
The lesion is hyperintense on T2-weighted MRI.
The lesion shows rim-like peripheral enhancement after contrast on MRI.
CT shows a hypodense cystic lesion.
CT shows no contrast enhancement of the lesion.
The normal pituitary gland enhances normally.
The pituitary stalk enhances normally.
The normal pituitary gland and stalk are displaced laterally to the right.
The lesion is separate from but adjacent to the pituitary.
These imaging features support a benign cystic sellar/suprasellar lesion rather than a solid pituitary neoplasm.
Neurologic examination is unremarkable despite chiasmal compression.
Ophthalmologic examination is unremarkable despite chiasmal compression.
Visual acuity is normal.
Fundoscopy is normal.
Visual fields are normal.
Pituitary hormone levels are normal.
The normal pituitary hormone levels argue against a functioning pituitary adenoma.
The normal pituitary hormone levels make significant pituitary stalk dysfunction less likely.
CBC is normal.
Chemistry is normal.
Urinalysis is normal.
The normal CBC, chemistry, and urinalysis provide no support for infection.
The normal CBC, chemistry, and urinalysis provide no support for inflammatory disease.
The normal CBC, chemistry, and urinalysis provide no support for systemic malignancy.
CT shows no calcification.
CT shows no solid enhancing component.
The absence of calcification or a solid enhancing component argues against some craniopharyngiomas.
The main differential for a cystic sellar/suprasellar lesion includes Rathke cleft cyst.
The main differential for a cystic sellar/suprasellar lesion includes craniopharyngioma.
The main differential for a cystic sellar/suprasellar lesion includes cystic pituitary adenoma.
The main differential for a cystic sellar/suprasellar lesion includes arachnoid cyst.
Rathke cleft cysts are typically benign cystic sellar lesions.
Rathke cleft cysts are often intrasellar with suprasellar extension.
Rathke cleft cysts can cause headache.
Rathke cleft cysts can displace the normal pituitary gland and stalk.
Rathke cleft cysts often show no endocrine abnormality.
MRI signal in Rathke cleft cysts can vary depending on cyst contents.
A T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense cyst with thin rim enhancement is compatible with Rathke cleft cyst.
Lack of a solid component supports Rathke cleft cyst.
Preservation of normal pituitary enhancement supports Rathke cleft cyst.
Craniopharyngioma can be cystic.
Craniopharyngioma can be suprasellar.
Craniopharyngioma can compress the optic chiasm.
In adults, craniopharyngiomas often have mixed solid-cystic components.
In adults, craniopharyngiomas often have more irregular enhancement.
Calcification is common on CT in craniopharyngioma.
This case’s CT showed a hypodense cystic lesion with no contrast enhancement.
This case has no mention of calcification.
This case has no mention of solid nodules.
These findings make craniopharyngioma less likely.
Cystic pituitary adenoma can undergo cystic degeneration.
Cystic pituitary adenoma can cause headache.
Cystic pituitary adenoma can cause chiasmal compression.
The normal pituitary gland and stalk are seen separately and displaced by the lesion.
Pituitary hormones are normal.
The lesion appears more like a distinct cyst than an adenoma arising from the gland itself.
An arachnoid cyst could produce a nonenhancing cystic suprasellar lesion with CSF-like signal and mass effect.
Rim-like peripheral enhancement is less typical for an arachnoid cyst.
The lesion’s sellar relationship with displacement of the pituitary is more characteristic of a Rathke cleft cyst.

The combination of chronic headache, a well-defined cystic sellar/suprasellar lesion, T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, thin rim enhancement, no solid enhancement on CT, normal pituitary labs, and lateral displacement of a normally enhancing pituitary gland and stalk most strongly supports Rathke cleft cyst.
Rathke cleft cyst is the high-probability differential diagnosis.
Craniopharyngioma is a medium-probability differential diagnosis.
Cystic pituitary adenoma is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
Arachnoid cyst is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
The final diagnosis is Rathke cleft cyst.
